Abstract
The accelerated pace of development in the Field of Quantum Computing is very alarming for many of the presently used 
cryptographic algorithms such as RSA and ECC underlying much of security in the modern world. This is an indication 
that the need for development of quantum-resistant algorithms especially for security in data integrity and communica-
tion in the environment driven by quantum computers, commonly referred to as Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). 
For addressing this, the Research presents a scientometric lenses on PQC to provide a systematic review of its related 
research terrain, thematic trends and key contributors for directionality purposes. In the scientific aspect, the work uses 
new-generation scientometric techniques, including co-words, thematic maps, and network diagrams based on 2874 
articles sourced from the WoS and SCOPUS databases, which were systematically evaluated using the PRISMA protocol 
in R Studio. Such an approach could help disentangle the publication profiles, collaborative structures, and emergent 
institutionalization of PQC research. Identified insights demonstrate that the growth pattern of PQC has become steeper, 
with the number of annual publications reaching 623 in 2023, where Florida Atlantic University and Tsinghua University 
are also the most active institutions. Despite this progress, major research gaps persist, particularly in scaling PQC algo-
rithms, cross-platform adaptability, and testing in real-world settings, which are essential for applications in constrained 
environments like IoT networks. Thus, this study sets a foundation of reference on PQC research and presents noble 
advice to scholars, legislators, and entrepreneurs. These findings make the case for constant development and reliable 
procedures to safeguard computational assets from new forms of attack posed by quantum computing and, in doing 
so, point to an exciting future in the post-quantum world.

1  Introduction
The rapid development of quantum computers creates unparalleled opportunities [1] but at the same time, it is a serious 
threat to many areas-above all, cryptography. Traditional cryptographic systems, including Rivest–Shamir–Adleman (RSA) 
and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) forming the backbone of international digital security [2, 3] so far, are vulnerable 
to the enormous processing powers of quantum computers [4]. Quantum computers show their capabilities through 
algorithms like Shor’s Algorithm that factor large numbers promptly, thereby demolishing the security foundation of 
RSA-that relies on the factors of integers being hard to compute. Similarly, Shor’s Algorithm applies disastrous impacts on 
ECC since discrete logarithmic problems can now be solved exponentially faster than classical algorithms; hence, secure 
communication, financial transactions and sensitive information protection worldwide are under heavy threat [5, 6].

The emergence of quantum computing poses a vital threat to these well-established encryption systems. Quantum 
computers powered by the rules of quantum mechanics could break widely used cryptographic algorithms and render 
security measures obsolete [7]. Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) has thus been very critical in these respects-a field 
of study concerning research into cryptographic algorithms that resist quantum attacks. PQC is specifically a domain 
of cryptography that focuses on developing algorithms that remain safe against a quantum computer. In the quantum 
challenge, Post-Quantum Cryptography should develop such cryptographic algorithms that will guarantee the security 
of our digital infrastructure against even the mighty computational power of quantum machines [8].
These scholars contribute to various areas of research and produce an extensive publication record that needs thor-
ough analysis to understand their real contribution) [9]. The research field of Post-Quantum Cryptography has been 
rapidly developing with scholars from all parts of the world contributing to the development of quantum-resistant 
encryption methods [10, 11]. Scientometrics is the quantitative analysis discipline of scientific publication [12] that is 
instrumental in mapping landscapes of research and underpin significant trends, contributors, and intellectual frame-
works. Scientometric methods let researchers chart the growth of a field, its emerging themes, and the impact of insti-
tutions, authors, and publications in an objective manner [13]. This analysis provides an overview of how the area of 
research is changing and who produces significant advancement.
With the growing interest in PQC, there is a serious lack of deep scientometric investigations that would systematically 
explore the intellectual structure of the field, its main contributors, and thematic trends. So far, most of the attempts 
undertaken were limited to basic bibliometric techniques, which cannot represent the depth and insight required for the 
understanding of PQC evolution. Given the pressing demand to make global digital infrastructure resistant to quantum 
attacks, the study should take a detailed mapping of the research landscape of PQC, determining the key actors, research 
centers, and promising directions for further development of this area. This paper offers a new scientometric analysis 
of PQC based on data from Web of Science and Scopus. Therefore, this study would follow the PRISMA framework for 
extracting and synthesizing the data with methodological accuracy. By applying high-level scientometric tools, the 
research gives an in-depth look at the growth of PQC, collaborative networks, top publications, and key authors. This 
paper establishes a new benchmark for understanding PQC through the identification of emerging trends and stating 
significant research gaps. It provides all the necessary knowledge about the development of the area and thus lays a 
pathway to further advancement and leads an international effort to secure systems based on cryptography in the 
quantum computing era.
PQC is a strictly specialized area of research comprising various forms of algorithmic classes expected to be resistant to 
the computation power of quantum attacks. These classes have lattice-based, code-based, and hash-based algorithms, 
with each of these systems basing some related security assumptions and providing the appropriate trade-offs [14]. Algo-
rithms are designed to provide long-term security in digital communications and data even with the threat of quantum 
attacks. Among these lattice-based algorithms [15] like CRYSTALS-Kyber and CRYSTALS-Dilithium are founded on math-
ematical complexity found in lattice problems known for their resistance power against Shor’s algorithms [16]. Algorithms 
rooted in coding theory, such as the McEliece cryptosystem [17], utilize error-correcting codes, which deliver robust 
security while frequently necessitating substantial key sizes. Conversely, hash-based algorithms like SPHINCS + obtain 
their security from cryptographic hash functions [18, 19], presenting a more straightforward, albeit slower, alternative. 
This variety underscores the continual endeavors to identify optimal methodologies for quantum-resistant cryptography, 
striking a balance among security, efficiency, and resource demands across various applications.
The potential risk posed by quantum computing to traditional cryptographic systems primarily revolves around the 
expected power of quantum computers to resolve intricate mathematical challenges that form the foundation of RSA 
and ECC encryption. Notably, Shor’s algorithm illustrates the theoretical proficiency of quantum computers to factor 
large integers and compute discrete logarithms at an exponentially accelerated rate compared to classical techniques, 
thereby directly threatening the security of RSA and ECC, which rely on these mathematical issues. The quantum threat 
is not limited to asymmetric cryptographic systems alone, Grover’s algorithm would pose a threat at least to some small 
extent to symmetric key cryptosystems because the algorithms reduce the time complexity of brute-force attacks from 
exponential time into a square root of time. The timeline is pretty unstable for the beginning of large-scale quantum com-
puters to perform these algorithms; however, recent progress illustrates that the threat may arise within coming decades. 
This urgency brings PQC at the forefront of cryptographic research because preparing for the quantum era demands 
pressing consideration of securing the global digital infrastructure before these quantum capabilities materialize.
PQC research is not easy to be practically implemented. In fact, to merge PQC algorithms with existing security infra-
structures, one has to face the disadvantages of key size and computational efficiency. PQC algorithms were shown 
to have much larger key sizes and encryption speeds as slow as classical cryptosystems [20], which illustrates that

2  Literature review
The fast growth of quantum computing has provoked a great deal of research in Post-Quantum Cryptography, which 
attempts to propose cryptographic methods that are resistant against quantum-based attacks. Chikouche & Ghadbane 
made one of the first evaluations of PQC schemes on smart mobile devices, analyzing them according to computational 
time, memory usage, and power consumption [22]. This study is a very useful basis for PQC in resource-constrained 
environments like those of mobile devices. But its restrictive limitation to mobile applications indicates that further 
extensive investigation into PQC performance would require an even greater canvas of various devices and networks.
PQC is also the focus of Mueller et al. on PQC while exploring the integration of PQC with the DNSSEC protocol. The 
DNA is an essential Internet security layer, whereby this case-driven analysis addresses the challenges that quantum 
threats bring to DNSSEC alone, such as compact signatures and efficient validation. While their research shows that PQC 
has lots of promise toward improving security for DNS, the lack of a direct replacement algorithm presents a gap that 
demands the development of flexible PQC solutions toward broader Internet protocols [23].
In another pioneering work, Djordjevic proposed a hybrid cryptographic system that integrated both QKD and PQC 
in order to achieve longer transmission distances and higher key rates. Although this is quite innovative, it is very case-
specific and surely questions its scalability for bigger networks. In this respect, talking to the literature, this work gives 
useful insights into the practical integration of quantum and post-quantum systems with high emphasis regarding the 
extension of hybrid cryptosystems in future research [24].
PQC’s adaptability is also explored by Debnath et al. who further study the adaptability of PQC by introducing a 
new multivariate-based functional encryption scheme, particularly important for secure inner product computations 
in cloud and IoT applications. Although the design focuses on non-adaptive security under the MQ problem, it directs 
attention to a potential research gap, especially in dynamic environments where challenges for security are bound to 
change over time [25].
The study by Yi Haibo: The work extends research in PQC into hardware security by using ML-based techniques for 
evaluating the side-channel vulnerabilities of PQC signatures. It happens to be one of the first applications of ML toward 
the analysis of attacks and their side channels by advancing a critical resilience aspect in physical attacks in implementa-
tions of PQC. However, the ML-based approach in that regard is still to be validated empirically [26].
PQC is involved in real-world contexts in connection with IoT, as is conducted by Septien-Hernandez et al. in the paper 
in 2022 [27], where PQC was critically analyzed. The study has been carried out by authors with the aim of comparing the 
performance of PQC algorithms while working on low-power devices for IoT, which expands perspectives concerning 
energy-efficient cryptographic solutions. Although it focused on IoT, the limited exploration of scalability in the study 
shows that future studies must test the flexibility of PQC for use in diverse applications.
Among the contributions, Li et al. designed a high-speed PQC processor dedicated to the CRYSTALS-Dilithium sig-
nature scheme [28]. This work enables the advancement of PQC in high-performance computing by way of enhanced 
speed using modular multiplication and parallel processing. After all, such intense reliance on hardware optimization 
questions its software flexibility, where adaptive solutions are in greater demand. Against this background, this research 
further underlines the potential of PQC in high-speed applications while pointing to the challenge of balancing hardware 
and software adaptability. In much the same vein, one comes across a performance analysis of PQC algorithms for digital 
signatures, namely CRYSTALS-Dilithium, Falcon, and SPHINCS + , by Opiłka et al. [29].
The study reveals the trade-offs between security and efficiency in indicating PQC algorithm selection to be made for 
the secure services in 5G/6G networks [29]. Yet, the lack of practical testing on different network infrastructures hints at

3  Research methodology
3.1  Scientometric analysis
Scientometric analysis is a method applied for the quantitative assessment of trends and patterns in the published lit-
erature. Scientometric analysis quantifies productivity in research and the development of scientific fields through the 
use of statistical and network analysis methods on scientific information. In this way, one reaches conclusions about the 
impact and influence of research outputs. It finds popular applications in attempts to understand research productiv-
ity and the development of scientific domains through statistical and network analysis of bibliographic information. 
The research that follows aims to carry out an extensive analysis of research contributions related to ’Post-Quantum 
Cryptography’, with Search String “"Post-Quantum Cryptography". In total, this dataset comprises 3492 research articles 
that were retrieved from Scopus and the Web of Science. More specifically, this dataset consists of 2573 papers in Bib-
TeX format, which were crawled from Scopus, and another 919 papers in plain text format, which were collected from 
WoS. It should be noted that August 9, 2024, was the date when data collection was performed. The present study aims, 
therefore, at underlining the main trends, topics, influential authors, institutions, and countries that have contributed 
to Post-Quantum Cryptography.
Though Scopus and Web of Science are extremely comprehensive and reputable sources that cover almost 90% of 
quality papers [31, 32], even this method is susceptible to selection bias. This method can inadvertently exclude newly 
emerging research, especially open-access papers and conference proceedings, which are often typified by the fast-mov-
ing field of PQC. Even though Scopus and Web of Science are a good foundation, arXiv, Google Scholar, or IEEE Xplore will 
enrich this database, and including these sources will, in future studies, increase the probability of incorporating emerg-
ing studies and conference publications that may yet not have been indexed in either Scopus or Web of Science [33, 34].
3.2  Extraction of data
The procedure of extracting data had its rationale in making sure relevant research publications are maximally obtained. 
Data is collected using the search “Post-Quantum Cryptography.” To ensure the dataset includes various literature on the 
application of Post-Quantum Cryptography, articles were sought from both Scopus and Web of Science. Data was further 
enriched through several preprocessing stages once it was collected and exported in the proper formats for analysis.

3.3  Preprocessing data and cleaning process
In order to provide accurate and high-quality scientometric analysis, it has done the following:
1.	 Data conversion from scopus: First of all, the conversion of the 2573 papers identified from Scopus was done to a 
compatible format in RStudio for further analysis.
2.	 Merging of the scopus and web of science data: After their conversion processes, papers from both Scopus and 
WoS were combined into one dataset. During this process, another 618 duplicate entries were found and removed, 
thus leaving a total of 2874 papers.
3.	 Final screening: After combining these datasets and cleaning, a screening process was conducted to make sure the 
papers fell into the scope of this research, it excludes 1372 papers. After this screening, a total of 1502 were included 
in this study.
3.3.1  Inclusion and exclusion criteria
•	 Inclusion criteria: Only post-quantum cryptography applications, algorithms, and developments were considered 
in the study.
•	 Exclusion criteria: Any paper that had not concentrated on cryptographic resilience against quantum threats were 
excluded. This includes general cryptography and any study that did not have a relation to quantum. The structured 
process of exclusion and inclusion ensured relevance and comprehensiveness.
3.4  Methods and tools used, including PRISMA
In this work, we will follow a well-articulated methodology to provide all-inclusive coverage of the available research for a 
comprehensive Scientometric profile on Post-Quantum Cryptography. The search was initiated from two major scientific 
databases: Web of Science, which contained 919 journal papers, and Scopus, which had a total of 2573 journal papers. 
In WoS, extracted data was exported to.txt data; in Scopus, the same is exported as a BibTeX file. Again, using RStudio, 
it was possible to merge the two datasets into one dataset [35]. The data was filtered to avoid duplication and make 
data formats consistent to ensure high quality data for subsequent analysis, which resulted in a final set of 1502 papers.
Several metrics were used to assess performance and gauge productivity and the impact of research in this domain 
[36]. Descriptive statistics provided an overview of some of the key indicators among them the number of publications, 
citation counts, and contributing authors. We analyzed yearly trends in publications and mapped their distribution by 
country, identifying the most-cited authors, institutions, and countries. Other metrics applied to provide further insights 
were cumulative publications per year, average citation per paper, and three-field plots. We also applied Bradford’s Law 
and Lotka’s Law to ascertain publication distributions and author productivity respectively [37], alongside the recogni-
tion of the most globally cited documents, in order to highlight leading research within the dataset.
Mapping techniques, through scientific means, visualized the field with respect to its relationships and structures 
[38]. This involved source and author impact assessment at a local level, geographic mapping of their distribution for 
respective authors, and co-word analysis for main themes and their relationships. Trends and topics in their change over 
time are illustrated by tree maps and word frequency analyses. Coupling maps, co-word networks, and thematic maps 
give a general view for the structure of themes and their evolution. Factorial analysis, country, author, and institutional 
collaboration networks, and other analyses provide an added dimension to our understanding of the research dynamics 
and collaboration patterns.
Biblioshiny was used for generating performance metrics and science maps. Data preprocessing and preliminary 
analysis were performed on RStudio [39]. More specifically, network visualization software like scientometric was run 
to generate detailed maps of scientometric networks. Network metrics and clustering methods are two enrichment 
techniques applied to estimate the relative relevance of research entities and to detect thematic clusters.
A methodical scientometric analytic methodology was employed, utilizing the subsequent instruments and 
techniques:
1.	 RStudio: The environment provided by RStudio was helpful in cleaning the data, screening them [40], and making 
some preliminary descriptive statistics, which provide information on the number of publications [41], the number

3.5  Performance evaluation, science mapping and network analysis
The performance evaluation utilized a technique for mapping performance and science.
1.	 Performance evaluation: The analysis of research involving an overview of various scientometric indicators included 
the number of published papers, citations per paper, and the h-index referring to authors, institutions, and countries. 
These indicators provided the necessary bases for measuring productivity and the impact of research related to PQC.
2.	 Science mapping: Network analysis has been carried out to explore the connection between research entities [42]. 
This covers:
•	 Citation analysis: It would provide information about the influential papers and top authors in the area.
•	 Co-citation analysis: mapping of intellectual structures that define thematic connections between a set of papers 
commonly co-cited [43].
•	 Co-word analysis: The co-occurrence of words could be studied to identify research trends and emerging themes 
related to PQC.
•	 Co-authorship analysis will look into the collaboration pattern amongst the authors and institutions, thus giving 
insights into the global research network.
3.6  Enrichment techniques
Network metrics applied to deepen the scientometric analysis will be described as follows:
•	 Degree centrality: A node’s connectedness within the research network is determined by the number of direct links it 
has with other nodes, such as authors, institutions, or nations.
•	 Betweenness centrality: Underlined nodes hold a crucial role in connecting disparate parts of the network and are vital 
in facilitating collaborations or knowledge transfer.
•	 Centrality closeness: It refers to the degree of ease with which a node reaches all other nodes within the network and 
thus provides insight into its accessibility and influence.
These methods enabled us to realize the structure of the research landscape, networks of collaboration, and thematic 
trends related to PQC. The present study provides a foundation for identifying priorities for the most important areas of future 
research and major contributors in this fast-evolving field.

5  Studies gaps and future research directions
5.1  Research gaps
1.	 Lack of robust practical implementations: There are only a few PQC algorithms developed, and very few of them 
are tested for true simulations. Most of the proposed algorithms are purely theoretical or at the simulation stage and 
not adequately tested in dynamic environments like IoT networks and clouds might provide vulnerabilities. The PQC 
Testing is needed for a practical and robust deployment within critical and resource-constrained infrastructures.
2.	 Concrete scalability and efficiency problems: Most PQC schemes suffer from inefficiency and lack scalability, 
making it impossible to use in systems of such large systems, like in the cloud infrastructures and IoT networks. 
Optimization research with special focus on High-Speed resource-limited environment is required for algorithmic 
performances. Hardware optimization and parallelization techniques can be used and studied in order to improve 
the efficiency and scalability even more.
3.	 Lack of integration of interdisciplinary studies: PQC puts together at least three disciplines into one. In the case 
presented, it has quantum computing, mathematics, and classical cryptography. There exists a very huge gap lying 
between disciplines where study can capture various fields to innovate PQC solutions. One specific gap especially 
lies in the capturing of insights from quantum physics in designing the cryptosystems to advance PQC research. 
Notably, interdisciplinary collaborations, in general, should be sought for unique problems such as the development 
of hybrid schemes both for classical and quantum-resistant methods.
4.	 Long-term security: The design of PQC Algorithms has been such that it can resist quantum attacks. However, 
there still remains uncertainty about long term security. Such algorithms may encounter drafted and unforeseen 
vulnerabilities with rising quantum capability. A lot of research work needs to be done in order to build adaptive 
cryptographic schemes responsive to the ultimate outcomes of quantum computing for sustained protection.
5.	 Challenges in standardization and adoption: There is not much standard protocols or frameworks in PQC; hence, 
major industries and services are not adapting much. Unless standards are realized, the organizations will never adopt 
the PQC solutions. Another key promising development—the NIST PQC competition and its follow-up to establish 
standardized PQC algorithms—remains unlikely with wider adoption efforts. Coordination between researchers, 
industrialists and policymakers is an absolute prerequisite to instill confidence in PQC solutions through recognized 
standards.
5.2  Future research directions
1.	 Actual implementation and testing of PQC algorithms: Future research should be implemented into testing 
PQC algorithms in real-world applications for some of the cases associated with Internet of Things networks, cloud 
computing, etc. Other critical infrastructures should emphasize exposing them to potential vulnerabilities and let 
them be strong under different conditions. In addition, further testing of PQC for industry-specific applications like 
blockchain and cloud security would further verify the algorithms for real life use.

concerning upwardly compatible studies toward schemes in cryptography working toward future quantum progress 
along with devising any mechanism capable of monitoring it over time and fixing it accordingly. There should always 
be evaluations conducted about how to keep moving forward with good protection over the quantum capabilities 
that are expanding.
5.	 Standardization and global adoption: There is a call for designing standardized protocols and frameworks of PQC 
that will make easier universal acceptance. Investigators have to identify collaborative engagement with industry 
stakeholders, policymakers, and international bodies driving the process of standardization. Global adaptation of PQC 
solutions will guarantee industries beginning to work on quantum-resistant cryptography with absolute conviction.
6.	 Integration with the broader PQC ecosystem: Hence, the work would be on evaluating those PQC solutions well 
fitted in existing infrastructures in cryptography specifically in respect of privacy, regulatory frameworks, and industry 
standards that PQC brings forward. Transitioning provider strategy toward a quantum-resistant cryptography future 
will be key for providers who want to ensure security in a post-quantum-enabled future.
6  Conclusion
Emergence and rapid innovation in quantum computing bring with themselves unexampled opportunities and 
behemothic challenges, more specifically concerning cybersecurity. Quantum technologies threaten traditional cryp-
tographic frameworks such as RSA and ECC, which so far have been the cornerstone of digital security. Motivated by 
this new quantum threat, the area of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC), which deals with developing cryptographic 
algorithms that are going to be resilient to a quantum attack, has evolved. PQC in such a changing scenario is an 
important area of research needed to help protect the global digital infrastructure against the nefarious effects of 
prospective quantum breaks.
This paper provides a new, comprehensive scientometric analysis of PQC research that provides crucial insights 
not available in conventional bibliometric studies. Through examination of publication trends, identification of key 
contributors, and mapping of emerging themes, this study captures the intellectual and collaborative structure of 
the field. The analysis differs from scholarship in the following aspects: subtle patterns of collaboration, thematic 
progressions, and influential works that inform PQC; it must be said that the current trends of interest in such areas as 
lattice-based cryptography, quantum-resistant key exchange mechanisms, and novel signature schemes underscore 
the rapid growth pace and responsiveness of PQC to the urgent need for quantum-resistant solutions.
The findings from this study demonstrate an exponential increase in PQC research, driven by global partnerships 
and pathbreaking work coming out of partners like Florida Atlantic University and Tsinghua University. The trends 
discussed here can be used as a roadmap for the actors involved, from researchers to policymakers to industry lead-
ers, identifying foundational papers and emergent areas of research that are most likely to help cross the quantum 
threat divide.
Prominent themes, such as lattice-based cryptography and signature schemes, do not only mean that the field is 
adaptable but also underpin its crucial significance in the advancement of digital security. The power of this study lies 
in that it points out the leading publications and collaborative networks, thus giving immediate insight and drivers 
for further research and development in PQC. Another significant gap this analysis points out is the practicableness 
of implementation, bridging interdisciplinary efforts and conforming to standard protocols. Of course, increased key

Abstract: The accelerated pace of development in the Field of Quantum Computing is very alarming for many of the presently used cryptographic algorithms such as RSA and ECC underlying much of security in the modern world. This is an indication that the need for development of quantum-resistant algorithms especially for security in data integrity and communica- tion in the environment driven by quantum computers, commonly referred to as Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). For addressing this, the Research presents a scientometric lenses on PQC to provide a systematic review of its related research terrain, thematic trends and key contributors for directionality purposes. In the scientific aspect, the work uses new-generation scientometric techniques, including co-words, thematic maps, and network diagrams based on 2874 articles sourced from the WoS and SCOPUS databases, which were systematically evaluated using the PRISMA protocol in R Studio. Such an approach could help disentangle the publication profiles, collaborative structures, and emergent institutionalization of PQC research. Identified insights demonstrate that the growth pattern of PQC has become steeper, with the number of annual publications reaching 623 in 2023, where Florida Atlantic University and Tsinghua University are also the most active institutions. Despite this progress, major research gaps persist, particularly in scaling PQC algo- rithms, cross-platform adaptability, and testing in real-world settings, which are essential for applications in constrained environments like IoT networks. Thus, this study sets a foundation of reference on PQC research and presents noble advice to scholars, legislators, and entrepreneurs. These findings make the case for constant development and reliable procedures to safeguard computational assets from new forms of attack posed by quantum computing and, in doing so, point to an exciting future in the post-quantum world.
